lxc_7842d4082e80a9e1.text: El Colacho, the Battle of the Oranges, Busójárás, Onbashira, Tinku, and Thaipusam offer six different traditions to explore.

lxc_8467b16215fb29c2.text: Look at each one through three simple ideas: its place, its actions, and its meaning.

lxc_b02c6bf89f37e2b6.text: El Colacho is a tradition in Castrillo de Murcia, a village near Burgos in Spain.

lxc_850a8de7794a10ac.text: It began in 1620, so it is more than 400 years old.

lxc_f7abb5eb52f5cca8.text: It takes place on the Sunday after Corpus Christi, a Christian celebration.

lxc_876b33234c38b015.text: The tradition is also called baby jumping.

lxc_2d06783022d71454.text: Babies born during the past year lie on mattresses in the street.

lxc_76831e4428f55e8a.text: A man dressed as the devil jumps over them.

lxc_7b0120901f63933f.text: This man is called El Colacho.

lxc_f6cce7cdc2a26ba4.text: The jump has a special meaning.

lxc_7fe8d76b9b5ba7af.text: People believe it takes away bad luck and evil.

lxc_88f5f240eaaa91c7.text: To understand this tradition, remember that the action and the belief belong together.

lxc_ec51d6cf2f2ac545.text: It is not simply a jump over mattresses.

lxc_b5f6a48785b20867.text: The Battle of the Oranges is the biggest part of the Historic Carnival of Ivrea.

lxc_d77470879e623db7.text: Ivrea is a town in Piedmont, in northern Italy.

lxc_7b4e07989557d6ac.text: The event lasts for three days before Carnival ends.

lxc_8b47e9f426096c91.text: Teams on foot throw oranges at throwers riding in carts.

lxc_aae77d177a044d18.text: The people throwing on foot are called aranceri.

lxc_501eab6e3dc81645.text: There are nine teams on foot, including the Diavoli and the Scacchi.

lxc_3004c14527b4ee20.text: Visitors who do not throw wear a red hat.

lxc_cad8d02ad3859720.text: Behind these actions is a story about the people of Ivrea standing up against a cruel ruler.

lxc_622f220c4f098c63.text: The event remembers that story through a shared activity.

lxc_e1f59b54ada8161d.text: Here, the meaning is different from El Colacho.

lxc_5ae4a0f90258dff9.text: It connects the town's celebration with a story about its people.

lxc_9c972b363799e59b.text: Busójárás is a six-day carnival in Mohács, a town in southern Hungary.

lxc_369fac71ba5cac00.text: It happens at the end of winter.

lxc_0ada4d2b8e666383.text: In 2026, it ran from 12 to 17 February and ended with a big bonfire, a large outdoor fire.

lxc_b3bfc0e3625e13ad.text: Men called busós wear scary wooden masks and sheepskin coats.

lxc_84b5bb04a0b90d72.text: These coats are made from sheep's skins.

lxc_9a342150e3e18a0b.text: The men also carry noisemakers, objects that make loud sounds.

lxc_681b7ae2a3d1f9f8.text: Masks, warm coats, and noise give this celebration its special character.

lxc_d2220fef05f4dd8e.text: The custom says goodbye to winter.

lxc_1271b47e53e057ac.text: The season is therefore part of its meaning, not just its date.

lxc_60e563944dc8b27c.text: In 2009, Busójárás joined UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

lxc_78acc9a20a5fbce5.text: This list recognises living traditions, including customs that communities continue to practise.

lxc_6bb51e34cf42b468.text: Onbashira is a festival of Suwa Taisha shrine around Lake Suwa in Nagano, Japan.

lxc_05ce4301fc78cc4b.text: A shrine is a place connected with religious belief.

lxc_e31a8d0ff42832e6.text: The festival is over 1,200 years old.

lxc_7e4f4840d6b556c9.text: It happens in the years of the Tiger and the Monkey, about once every six years.

lxc_cb52dc485d28c834.text: It was last held in 2022, and the next festival is in 2028.

lxc_ecefbc9de26e053a.text: Unlike the other traditions described so far, it is not a yearly event.

lxc_0a89ae02829aa827.text: People move 16 huge fir trees from the mountains to the shrine.

lxc_c136996f965f9387.text: The trees are over 150 years old and about 17 metres tall.

lxc_ca62c3f6036566b7.text: Riders ride the logs down steep slopes.

lxc_fbcf1b7f20f3388c.text: The shrine is at the centre of the festival, and moving these enormous trees is its shared task.

lxc_82f691e5916dbc2a.text: Tinku is an Andean ritual from northern Potosí in Bolivia.

lxc_70d0a7306ffe9762.text: A ritual is an activity with a special meaning that people repeat.

lxc_9bc3e28d2b8fea75.text: The best-known Tinku takes place in Macha during the Fiesta de la Cruz.

lxc_d238a118d15830c4.text: In 2026, it was on 3 and 4 May.

lxc_f5301d88e181d6c1.text: Communities come to the town's main square with music, colourful clothes, and dance.

lxc_8ff9e43d0d61fe2a.text: The ritual is a meeting between two groups of the community.

lxc_0f9dab543a97a2f3.text: People believe it brings a good harvest, meaning a good amount of food gathered from the fields.

lxc_c30bfe254e533580.text: Tinku is also a famous dance at carnival in Oruro.

lxc_ad63c45a41a9d7bf.text: Its name therefore connects with both a community ritual and a dance.

lxc_3b45f7ae08555de8.text: In Macha, hope for the harvest is central to its meaning.

lxc_5ab70d94c7b29c55.text: Thaipusam is a Hindu festival for Lord Murugan, celebrated by Tamil people.

lxc_d3917f0e8c6bafb9.text: Its biggest celebration is at Batu Caves, near Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia.

lxc_334ec21dbfb20b6e.text: Before the festival, more than 2.5 million visitors were expected at Batu Caves.

lxc_67f02530ad8412fd.text: That was an expectation, not a final visitor count.

lxc_7c8cbef41ab936ce.text: Devotees, people strongly committed to their religion, climb 272 colourful steps to the temple in the cave.

lxc_809f52ec28e8d704.text: Many carry a kavadi, a decorated frame, or pots of milk.

lxc_2fb892880ad4a2d5.text: Religious belief is central to this festival.

lxc_4bb02f7de70b1b05.text: The steps, the things people carry, and the temple visit are parts of the celebration for Lord Murugan.

lxc_b4d91a7ebe5a683e.text: Understanding that purpose helps us see more than a large crowd or colourful steps.
